tools.hv_spec_set: Create or update desired state for a project, including runtime configuration and infrastructure. New runtime keys must cover every non-local environment with matching services unless envVarExceptions explicitly documents that a key does not apply. Hypervibe never copies values between environments. This is the source of truth that hv_plan diffs against live infrastructure. When run inside a git worktree, Hypervibe writes .hypervibe/spec.json. Merges by default; pass replace=true to overwrite or null to delete a key.
tools.hv_spec_get: Read the current desired-state spec and revision for a project. If .hypervibe/spec.json exists in the current git worktree, it is treated as the shared desired state and synced into the local cache.
tools.hv_plan: Diff the spec against live infrastructure (observed where the provider supports it) and return an executable plan. Do not call hv_plan as a workaround after hv_status/hv_connections_list reports a missing required connection. Use hv_connect only when a safe credentialsRef is already available; otherwise explain the blocked task and offer to connect credentials the user already controls or prepare a value-free owner handoff. Do not assume provider membership. Repo-backed .hypervibe/spec.json and non-secret .hypervibe/bindings.json are used when present. The returned planId is required by hv_apply. Delegated secret slots declared by the spec accept values only through secretRefs={KEY:"env:NAME"|"dotenv:/absolute/path/.env#KEY"|"file:/absolute/path"|"<manager>://..."}; values are resolved locally, encrypted into that plan, and never returned. Ordinary envVars and env files cannot override delegated keys. By default, .env.<env> then repo .env are considered as deploy input in envFile.mode="runtime": high-confidence app runtime keys are encrypted into the plan and synced to hosting, while provider/control-plane credentials, local-only values, and unselected local junk are skipped with key-name warnings. If repo .env exists and .env.<env> is missing, hv_plan creates it while omitting envFile.exclude and delegated-secret keys. Optional services=[...] produces a partial deploy plan restricted to those spec services; delegated secret inputs require a full plan.
tools.hv_status: Show desired vs observed infrastructure state for an environment: drift, unmanaged resources, blocked connections, managed database-variable attachment, and observed service endpoints. inSync means configuration convergence only; runtimeHealth remains unverified until hv_health or worker log/error evidence is checked. Uses repo-backed .hypervibe/spec.json/.hypervibe/bindings.json when present. Read-only; does not persist a plan.
tools.hv_apply: Apply a plan produced by hv_plan. Rejects stale plans (spec changed, infrastructure changed, plan expired, or already applied). Confirm-gated billable/destructive actions run only when their action ids are passed in confirmActions. Legacy confirmDestroy is still accepted for database destroys.
tools.hv_inspect: Read-only provider inspection for forensics/adoption planning. Currently Railway only. Omit name/railwayProjectId to list projects; pass name or railwayProjectId to inspect environments, services, components, storage buckets, and env var names. Never writes Hypervibe local state or provider resources.
tools.hv_import: Adopt already-deployed provider infrastructure into Hypervibe local/repo state (currently Railway). Adoption writes explicit Hypervibe project/environment/service/component/storage bindings. For read-only provider data, use hv_inspect. Not for creating new infrastructure (use hv_spec_set + hv_apply).
tools.hv_destroy: Delete LOCAL Hypervibe records only: a project (cascade), an environment, or a service (including its platform binding). Never touches provider resources — to destroy live infrastructure, remove it from the spec with hv_spec_set, then run hv_plan and hv_apply. Data-bearing destroys are confirm-gated with confirmDestroy. Without confirm=true this returns CONFIRM_REQUIRED listing exactly what local records would be deleted.
tools.hv_connect: Manage provider connections. action="add" (default) stores credentials and immediately verifies them; action="verify" re-verifies an existing connection; action="remove" deletes one; action="prepare" runs one-time cloud account preparation (Cloud Run: enables required GCP APIs and grants deploy IAM roles using one-time admin credentials that are never stored — preview first, then pass confirm=true). Credentials are encrypted at rest and never returned. Recommended: use credentialsRef="env:NAME" for exported tokens, credentialsRef="dotenv:/absolute/path/.env#KEY" for existing .env files, credentialsRef="file:/absolute/path" for JSON credentials, or a secret-manager ref like 1password://vault/item#field. For GitHub, NODE_AUTH_TOKEN, HYPERVIBE_GITHUB_TOKEN, and HYPERVIBE_GITHUB_PACKAGES_TOKEN are aliases when only one distinct value is available. Raw credentials={...} is still accepted if the user intentionally wants to enter credentials in chat.
tools.hv_connections_list: List stored provider connections (provider, scope, status, last verified — never credentials) plus all connectable providers grouped by category.
tools.hv_deploy: Deploy services to an environment (staging, production, etc.). Plan-gated: builds a plan from the spec and applies it immediately; the planId and applyRunId are returned for the audit trail. Delegated secret slots accept values only through secretRefs={KEY:"env:NAME"|"dotenv:/absolute/path/.env#KEY"|"file:/absolute/path"|"<manager>://..."}; values are resolved locally and encrypted into the plan. Ordinary envVars and env files cannot override delegated keys. By default, .env.<env> then repo .env are considered as deploy input in envFile.mode="runtime". Requires a spec (hv_spec_set). Protected environments require confirm=true.
tools.hv_rollback: Rollback an environment through one plan-authorized command. Managed GitHub Actions deploys restore the previous verified exact-SHA release (or toSha) and return pending until the workflow is verified with hv_ci_status; direct provider deploys retain toRunId rollback. Database migrations and provider-side manual configuration are never reversed implicitly. Protected environments require confirm=true.
tools.hv_logs: Fetch logs and delivery status: runtime service logs, build logs, recent deployments, or Stripe webhook endpoint status.
tools.hv_errors: Surface production errors: list recent error log lines or summarize error and deployment health per service.
tools.hv_health: HTTP health-check a deployed service or an explicit URL. Project-backed checks also surface latest deployment failures across every bound environment when provider connections are available; unknown provider observations never count as healthy.
tools.hv_db_query: Run one bounded SQL statement against a database. Hypervibe uses an existing reachable endpoint or acquires provider-owned operation-scoped access (such as a connector, TCP proxy, or temporary firewall rule), then releases only access it created and reports cleanup status. SELECT is database-enforced read-only by default; allowMutations=true enables INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL. Multi-statement SQL is always rejected.
tools.hv_db_url: Get the database connection URL for an environment. Values are always masked in command output to avoid leaking credentials into transcripts or terminals.
tools.hv_secrets_set: Set secrets and environment variables. NEVER pass sensitive values via value/vars — they appear in the chat transcript; use secretRef (env:NAME, dotenv:/absolute/path/.env#KEY, file:/absolute/path, or a secret-manager ref — read locally, never enters chat) or generate=true for a new server-side random secret. target="hosting" (default) sets env vars on the deployed environment; destinations explicitly shares one resolved/generated value across selected environment/service targets. "manager" stores values in a secret manager (vault/aws-secrets/doppler — 1password and bitwarden are resolve-only: manage values there, then use target="mapping"); "mapping" maps a secretRef to an env var resolved at deploy time; "github" sets a GitHub Actions repository secret, or an environment secret when env is provided. remove=true deletes (mapping/github targets).
tools.hv_secrets_get: Read a secret (from a secret manager) or a hosting env var. Values are always masked in command output to avoid leaking credentials into transcripts or terminals.

tools.insert_data:
Inserts data into an MSSQL Database table. Supports both single record insertion and multiple record insertion using standard SQL INSERT with VALUES clause.
FORMAT EXAMPLES:
Single Record Insert:
{
  "tableName": "Users",
  "data": {
    "name": "John Doe",
    "email": "john@example.com",
    "age": 30,
    "isActive": true,
    "createdDate": "2023-01-15"
  }
}
Multiple Records Insert:
{
  "tableName": "Users", 
  "data": [
    {
      "name": "John Doe",
      "email": "john@example.com", 
      "age": 30,
      "isActive": true,
      "createdDate": "2023-01-15"
    },
    {
      "name": "Jane Smith",
      "email": "jane@example.com",
      "age": 25, 
      "isActive": false,
      "createdDate": "2023-01-16"
    }
  ]
}
GENERATED SQL FORMAT:
- Single: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (@param1, @param2)
- Multiple: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (@param1, @param2), (@param3, @param4), ...
IMPORTANT RULES:
- For single record: Use a single object for the 'data' field
- For multiple records: Use an array of objects for the 'data' field
- All objects in array must have identical column names
- Column names must match the actual database table columns exactly
- Values should match the expected data types (string, number, boolean, date)
- Use proper date format for date columns (YYYY-MM-DD or ISO format)

tools.design_to_code:
【设计稿转代码的唯一入口】当用户提到 .octo、index.json、设计稿、Figma、Octo，或要求"转化/转换/生成 前端页面代码"时，必须首先调用本工具。无需先调用 get_context_bundle 或 component_search，本工具已内置组件识别和规范获取。

⚠️ 禁止用 read_file 直接读取 .octo/ 下的 JSON 文件（文件极大，会浪费 token）。直接调用本工具即可，工具内部自动读取、解析、转换。

将 .octo/ 目录下的设计稿 JSON 转换为精简 DSL、React 脚手架（CSS + JSX）或 Vue SFC，自动推断 flex 布局和 CSS 样式，识别组件库组件并联动返回 Props 规范。

- 不传 file：列出 .octo/ 下所有可用文件名
- 传 file + outputMode：转换指定设计稿，返回结构化数据 + 组件规范（如有匹配）

⚠️ 调用本工具后，必须完成以下全部步骤才算任务完成，缺少任何一步都不算完成：

== html 模式（React）==
第一步（复制写入）：将返回的 styles.css 和 Page.tsx 逐字原样写入项目文件，禁止修改任何内容。
第二步（语义化改造）：在已写入的文件上修改：
  a. 只改 n- 开头的独立类名（如 n-33-946、n-rel-33-945、n-split-33-xxx）：参考对应元素的 data-name 属性理解其含义，替换为语义化名称（如 task-goal、title-bar）。styles.css 中的选择器同步修改，样式值保持不变
  b. s- 开头的共享类名（如 s-729846、s-02dea1）是多个元素共用的，禁止修改、禁止拆分、禁止重命名
  c. layout-node、flex-row-start、flex-col-center、btn、text、icon、vector 等布局类禁止修改
  d. 删除所有 data-name 属性

== devUI 模式（Vue）==
第一步（复制写入）：将返回的 Page.vue 逐字原样写入项目文件，禁止修改任何内容。
第二步（语义化改造）：在已写入的文件上修改：
  a. 只改 n- 开头的独立类名，<style scoped> 中的选择器同步修改，样式值不变
  b. s- 开头的共享类名禁止修改
  c. 布局类禁止修改
  d. 组件标签及其 props 禁止修改
  e. 删除所有 data-name 属性

只有第一步和第二步全部完成，才能结束任务。不要添加交互事件，不要修改任何 CSS 样式值。
tools.fetch_design_data:
从 Octo 平台下载设计稿到本地 .octo/ 目录，供 design_to_code 工具使用。

传入 input 参数即可，工具自动识别类型：
- 包含 ## 的字符串（如 "##53085E4C##"）→ 分享口令模式，下载 ZIP 并原样解压到 .octo/，无需配置 Token
- 其他字符串（如 "9E5B01GS_546"）→ fileKey 模式，通过 getDSL 下载设计稿

使用流程：
1. 调用本工具下载设计稿：`fetch_design_data({ input: "##53085E4C##" })`
2. 调用 `design_to_code({ file: "xxx" })` 转换为代码

不传 input 时列出本地已有文件。

⚠️ 禁止在设计稿场景中首先调用本工具。当用户提到 .octo、设计稿、Octo 时，必须先调用 design_to_code 获取设计稿数据，design_to_code 已内置组件识别。本工具仅用于 design_to_code 之后补充组件信息。

tools.hunt_issues:
Discover open source issues on GitHub that match your skills and interests.

This tool searches for "good first issue" and "help wanted" labeled issues across repositories.
You can filter by programming language (e.g., Rust, Go, TypeScript), keywords in issue titles,
and minimum repository stars to find quality projects. Use this to explore opportunities before
diving deeper with analyze_repo.

TYPICAL WORKFLOW:
1. hunt_issues {language: "rust", min_stars: 100} → Find beginner Rust issues in established repos
2. analyze_repo {repo: "owner/name"} → Study the codebase you found
3. scaffold_solution → Generate starter code
4. claim_issue → Let maintainers know you're working on it

PRACTICAL EXAMPLES:
- Find Zig issues: hunt_issues {language: "zig", limit: 5}
- Search for CLI-related work: hunt_issues {keywords: "cli", min_stars: 50}
- Expand search beyond typical labels: hunt_issues {labels: "good-first-issue,help-wanted"}
tools.analyze_repo:
Clone and analyze a repository's structure, build system, and contributing guidelines.

This tool performs a deep dive into a GitHub repository to understand how to contribute.
It clones the repo (or updates existing clone), then provides:
- Project structure and key directories
- Build system and dependencies (detects Cargo.toml, package.json, build.zig, etc.)
- Contributing guidelines and conventions
- Open issues summary
- Code patterns used in the project

TYPICAL WORKFLOW:
1. hunt_issues → Find an interesting issue
2. analyze_repo {repo: "owner/name"} ← You are here
3. scaffold_solution → Generate starter implementation
4. claim_issue → Comment on the issue

PRACTICAL EXAMPLES:
- Analyze zigtools/zls: analyze_repo {repo: "zigtools/zls"}
- Analyze and focus on issue #42: analyze_repo {repo: "owner/name", issue_number: 42}

The analysis includes CONTRIBUTING.md content, key file detection, and directory structure.
Cloned repos are cached in ~/Developer/bug-hunter-repos/ for reuse.
tools.scaffold_solution:
Generate a starter implementation scaffold tailored to the project type.

This tool creates boilerplate code and project structure for solving a specific issue.
Based on project type detection (Rust, Zig, Go, TypeScript, Python, etc.), it generates:
- Skeleton implementation files with proper syntax and conventions
- NOTES.md with issue details, analysis, and implementation checklist
- Test file templates matching project conventions
- TODO list and next steps

TYPICAL WORKFLOW:
1. hunt_issues → Find an issue
2. analyze_repo → Understand the codebase
3. scaffold_solution {repo: "owner/name", issue_number: 42} ← You are here
4. Review NOTES.md in the _scaffold_issue_42 directory
5. Study the actual codebase
6. Implement your solution using the scaffold as a starting point

PRACTICAL EXAMPLE:
- Scaffold for Rust project: scaffold_solution {repo: "rust-lang/rust", issue_number: 123}
  Creates: implementation_title.rs, tests, and NOTES.md with TODOs

The scaffold is created in _scaffold_issue_<number>/ directory (or custom output_dir).
Use it as a starting point, then move completed files to appropriate locations in the repo.
tools.claim_issue:
Post a comment on a GitHub issue to let maintainers know you're working on it.

This tool helps you communicate your intent to the maintainers before starting work.
It posts a comment (default or custom) indicating you've analyzed the codebase and are
beginning implementation. This prevents duplicate effort and signals active work.

IMPORTANT: Requires GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable with 'repo' scope permissions.
Get your token at: https://github.com/settings/tokens

TYPICAL WORKFLOW:
1. hunt_issues → Find an issue
2. analyze_repo → Study the codebase
3. scaffold_solution → Generate starter code
4. claim_issue {repo: "owner/name", issue_number: 42} ← You are here
5. Implement your solution
6. Submit a pull request

DEFAULT MESSAGE:
"I'd like to work on this issue! I've analyzed the codebase and am starting on an implementation."

PRACTICAL EXAMPLE:
- Claim with default message: claim_issue {repo: "zigtools/zls", issue_number: 123}
- Claim with custom message: claim_issue {repo: "...", issue_number: 123, message: "I'll work on this using approach X..."}
tools.generate_chant_spec:
Generate a Chant spec from a GitHub issue for spec-driven development.

This tool bridges GitHub issues and Chant's spec-driven workflow. It creates a markdown spec file
that Chant agents can execute. The spec auto-extracts:
- Issue context and acceptance criteria
- Target files likely to need changes
- GitHub labels (converted to Chant labels)
- Issue URL and background

CHANT WORKFLOW (Spec-Driven Development):
1. hunt_issues → Find an issue
2. analyze_repo → Understand the code
3. generate_chant_spec {repo: "owner/name", issue_number: 42} ← You are here
4. Edit the .md spec to refine acceptance criteria
5. Use 'chant split' to break into focused sub-specs
6. Run 'chant work <spec-id>' to have AI agents implement

PRACTICAL EXAMPLE:
- Generate spec: generate_chant_spec {repo: "zig-lang/zig", issue_number: 15000}
- Output: .chant/specs/zig-lang-zig-implement-feature.md
- Edit the spec to improve acceptance criteria
- Split: chant split zig-lang-zig-implement-feature
- Execute: chant work zig-lang-zig-implement-feature.1

RELATED TOOLS:

tools.research_workflow:
Execute Chant's two-phase workflow: research then implementation.

This is the enterprise-grade approach for complex issues. It creates two interdependent specs:

   - Creates RESEARCH_<issue_number>.md with findings

- <date>-impl-500.md spec (implementation phase, depends on research)

tools.call_rest_api:
Makes a REST API call to any registered service with automatic authentication.

SUPPORTED SERVICES (REST only):
- datadog - Monitoring and observability platform
- github - Repository and code management
- jsonplaceholder - Testing API
- httpbin - HTTP testing service
- coingecko, coinbase, coincap - Cryptocurrency data
- tmdb - Movie database
- (See get_service_stats for full list)

WHEN TO USE:
- User asks for specific data from a REST service (NOT GraphQL services)
- After discovering an endpoint with explore_rest_patterns
- When you know the exact API endpoint path and service name

WRONG TOOL:
- For GraphQL services (countries, spacex), use call_graphql instead

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Whether the API call succeeded
- statusCode (number): HTTP status code (200 = success, 404 = not found, 401 = auth failed, etc.)
- data (any): The API response body (JSON, text, or other format)
- headers (object): Response headers from the API
- requestDetails: Information about the request (URL, method, duration in ms)
- error (if failed): AI-friendly error with recovery suggestions and alternative tools

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- statusCode 200-299: Success - use the data field for your answer
- statusCode 404: Resource not found - suggest alternatives or check if ID/path is correct
- statusCode 401/403: Authentication/permission issue - verify service credentials
- statusCode 429: Rate limited - wait before retrying, or reduce request frequency
- statusCode 500-599: Server error - try again later or use alternative service
- Check error.recovery.suggestions for AI-actionable next steps

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "coingecko",
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/api/v3/simple/price",
  "queryParams": { "ids": "bitcoin", "vs_currencies": "usd" }
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only works with services configured in services.json (use get_service_stats to list)
- Cannot call arbitrary URLs (security restriction)
- Respects service rate limits and timeouts
- Path parameters must be substituted using pathParams field
- Authentication is automatic but requires valid credentials in environment
tools.call_graphql:
Executes a GraphQL query or mutation against a registered service with automatic authentication.

SUPPORTED SERVICES (GraphQL only):
- countries - Country information (public API)
- spacex - Space missions and launches (public API)

WHEN TO USE:
- User asks for data from a GraphQL API (e.g., "get country information", "list SpaceX launches")
- After using introspect_graphql_schema to discover available fields
- When you need to fetch related data in a single request (GraphQL strength)
- For mutations that create/update data via GraphQL

WRONG TOOL:
- For REST services (datadog, github, etc.), use call_rest_api instead
- If you try a REST service with this tool, you'll get WRONG_API_TYPE error

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Whether the GraphQL query executed successfully
- data (any): The GraphQL response data matching your query structure
- errors (array): GraphQL errors if query failed (field errors, validation errors, etc.)
- aiError (if failed): AI-friendly error with recovery suggestions
- requestDetails: Operation name and duration in ms

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- success=true: Use data field directly (structure matches your query)
- errors array present: Check error messages for field/validation issues
- Use introspect_graphql_schema if you get "field doesn't exist" errors
- Check aiError.recovery for alternative tools or next steps
- GraphQL returns partial data even with errors (check both data and errors)

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "countries",
  "query": "query GetCountry($code: ID!) { country(code: $code) { name capital currency } }",
  "variables": { "code": "US" },
  "operationName": "GetCountry"
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only works with GraphQL services configured in services.json
- Requires valid GraphQL syntax (use introspect_graphql_schema to see schema)
- Cannot execute subscriptions (queries and mutations only)
- Variables must match query parameter types exactly
- Authentication is automatic but requires valid credentials
tools.introspect_graphql_schema:
Discovers the complete GraphQL schema of a service including types, queries, mutations, and fields.

WHEN TO USE:
- BEFORE making GraphQL queries to unknown APIs (discover available fields first)
- User asks "what data is available" from a GraphQL service
- You get GraphQL errors about unknown fields (re-introspect to see current schema)
- To explore a new GraphQL API without documentation
- When building complex queries (see all available fields and relationships)

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Whether introspection succeeded
- schema (object): Simplified GraphQL schema with:
  - queryType: Available queries (read operations)
  - mutationType: Available mutations (write operations)
  - subscriptionType: Available subscriptions (if supported)
  - types: All custom types with fields, args, descriptions
- errors (if failed): GraphQL introspection errors
- aiError (if failed): AI-friendly error with recovery suggestions

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- schema.queryType.fields: List all available read operations
- schema.mutationType.fields: List all available write operations
- Each field shows: name, type, args (parameters), description
- Use field types to construct correct GraphQL queries
- Field args show required vs optional parameters

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "countries",
  "typeName": "Country",
  "includeDeprecated": false
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only works with GraphQL services that allow introspection (some disable it for security)
- Large schemas may take 5-10 seconds to introspect
- Only shows schema structure, not actual data
- Use call_graphql to fetch actual data after discovering schema
tools.explore_rest_patterns:
Attempts to discover REST API endpoints using common patterns when the exact path is unknown.

**⚠️ WARNING: DO NOT USE THIS TOOL FOR SERVICES WITH QUERY BUILDER TEMPLATES**

**IMPORTANT USAGE RULES:**
1. **NEVER use for DataDog, GitHub, Stripe** - These have templates via build_query
2. **NEVER use when build_query returns confidence > 0.5** - Use the returned query directly
3. **ONLY use for completely unknown/undocumented APIs** without templates
4. **ONLY use as LAST RESORT** when build_query fails or returns low confidence

**Why NOT to use this tool:**
- Only tests GET requests (misses POST-only endpoints like DataDog queries)
- Takes 2-4 seconds to test 12 patterns
- Often finds wrong endpoints (e.g., ingestion instead of query endpoints)
- build_query with templates is faster and more accurate

WHEN TO USE (RARE):
- Discovering endpoints for custom internal APIs without templates
- User explicitly asks to "explore available endpoints"
- build_query returns confidence < 0.5 AND you need to discover alternatives

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Whether pattern discovery found any working endpoints
- patterns (array): Successfully discovered endpoints with:
  - pattern: The URL pattern that worked (e.g., "/api/v1/posts")
  - statusCode: HTTP response code (200, 404, etc.)
  - method: HTTP method used (GET, POST, etc.)
  - responseType: Response format (JSON, XML, text)
  - sampleFields: Key field names found in response
- totalAttempted/successful: Discovery statistics (e.g., "tried 12, found 3")

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- patterns array: Each entry is a working endpoint you can use with call_rest_api
- statusCode 200: Endpoint works and returns data - use this pattern
- Check sampleFields to understand what data the endpoint returns
- Use analyze_rest_response for deeper analysis of successful endpoints
- Multiple patterns may work - choose the most specific one

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "jsonplaceholder",
  "resource": "posts",
  "resourceId": "1"
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only tries common REST patterns (12 default patterns: /resource, /api/resource, etc.)
- May take 10-30 seconds for full discovery (tests multiple patterns)
- Some APIs block discovery attempts (return 403 Forbidden or 429 Rate Limited)
- Does not guarantee endpoints are officially supported or documented
- Custom patterns may not be discovered
tools.analyze_rest_response:
Analyzes REST API responses to understand structure, identify patterns, and discover related endpoints.

WHEN TO USE:
- After receiving a REST API response you need to understand
- To discover pagination patterns, HAL links, or embedded resources
- When response structure is complex or unclear
- To find related endpoints based on response data
- Before making multiple similar API calls (understand structure first)

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Analysis completed successfully
- analysis (object): Detailed response analysis with:
  - responseType: "object", "array", or "primitive"
  - schema: Generated JSON schema of the response structure
  - pagination: Detected pagination pattern (page-based, offset-based, cursor-based, or none)
  - halLinks: Discovered HAL links (_links) to related resources
  - embeddedResources: Nested data structures in the response
  - relatedEndpoints: Suggested API endpoints inferred from response data
  - suggestions: LLM-friendly recommendations for next steps

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- schema: Use this to understand field types and structure for future calls
- pagination.type: Shows how to request next/previous pages (check pagination.nextPageParams)
- halLinks: Direct links you can call with call_rest_api
- relatedEndpoints: Suggested endpoints based on IDs/references in response
- Combine with explore_rest_patterns for comprehensive API discovery

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "jsonplaceholder",
  "response": { "id": 1, "userId": 10, "title": "Post title", "body": "..." },
  "endpoint": "/posts/1"
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only analyzes structure, does not validate data correctness or completeness
- May not detect custom or non-standard pagination schemes
- Requires response to be JSON (cannot analyze XML, CSV, or plain text)
- HAL link detection only works if API follows HAL specification

Discover all available datasets/services with their capabilities and metadata.

tools.build_query:
Build service-specific API query from natural language intent.

This tool translates natural language investigation intents (e.g., "Find all 500 errors in production API from the last 24 hours") into service-specific API queries that can be executed with call_rest_api or call_graphql.

**IMPORTANT USAGE:**
- **USE THE RETURNED QUERY DIRECTLY** - Do NOT explore or try alternative endpoints
- **HIGH CONFIDENCE (>0.8)**: Use the query immediately with call_rest_api/call_graphql
- **MEDIUM CONFIDENCE (0.5-0.8)**: Review the explanation, then use the query
- **LOW CONFIDENCE (<0.5)**: Check alternatives or ask user to clarify intent
- **DO NOT use explore_rest_patterns** for services with templates (DataDog, GitHub, Stripe)

**For Multi-Entity Investigation:**
If you need to query multiple entity types (e.g., traces + monitors + metrics):
1. Call build_query SEPARATELY for each entity type
2. Use the returned queries directly (one call_rest_api per entity)
3. Then correlate results using summarize_multi_api_results

Example: To investigate an incident in DataDog:
- build_query("Find traces for service X") → call_rest_api with returned query
- build_query("Find monitors for service X") → call_rest_api with returned query
- build_query("Get metrics for service X") → call_rest_api with returned query
- summarize_multi_api_results to correlate all data

**Key Features:**
- Auto-detects target service from intent (DataDog, GitHub, Stripe, etc.)
- Translates to service-specific query format
- Returns confidence score indicating query accuracy
- Suggests alternatives for ambiguous intents
- Supports complex queries with filters, time ranges, and aggregations

**Intent Patterns Supported:**
- Error monitoring: "Find 500 errors in production", "Count errors by service"
- Performance: "Show slow requests", "Average latency for auth service"
- APM/Traces: "Find traces for service X", "Show spans with errors"
- Monitors: "Get monitor status", "Find triggered monitors"
- Metrics: "Query CPU usage", "Get memory metrics for service X"
- Infrastructure: "Check kubernetes pods", "Get database metrics"
- GitHub: "List open issues", "Show commits from last week"
- Stripe: "Find failed charges", "List unpaid invoices"

**Example Intents:**
- "Find all 500 errors in production API from the last 24 hours"
- "Count errors in staging from last week"
- "Show top 10 slow requests in auth service"
- "Find traces for mcu-claims-aggregate-api service"
- "Get monitor status for production environment"
- "Query CPU metrics for kubernetes pods"
- "List open issues in my repository"
- "Find failed charges from last month"

**Output:**
Returns a structured query that can be directly passed to call_rest_api or call_graphql, along with:
- Confidence score (0-1) indicating query accuracy
- Human-readable explanation of what the query does
- Alternative interpretations (if confidence < 0.8)
- **IMPORTANT**: The restQuery or graphqlQuery field contains the COMPLETE, READY-TO-USE query

**Use Cases:**
- Rapid investigation query building
- Natural language to API query translation
- Multi-service investigation workflows
- Query template discovery

**Related Tools:**
- call_rest_api: Execute the generated REST query
- call_graphql: Execute the generated GraphQL query
- summarize_multi_api_results: Correlate results from multiple queries
- discover_datasets: Find available services and capabilities
tools.save_api_pattern:
Saves a successful API interaction pattern for future reference and reuse by AI agents.

WHEN TO USE:
- After successfully calling an API (save the working pattern for reuse)
- To remember working API patterns for similar future requests
- Building a knowledge base of tested and validated API calls
- When you want other AI instances to benefit from your discoveries

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Pattern saved successfully
- pattern (object): The saved pattern with auto-generated ID and metadata
- message: Confirmation message or error details if save failed

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- success=true: Pattern is saved and immediately searchable via search_learned_patterns
- Pattern includes: name, service, apiType, request structure, tags
- Saved patterns track: usage count, last used timestamp, success rate
- Use search_learned_patterns to find this pattern later

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "name": "Get Bitcoin Price from CoinGecko",
  "service": "coingecko",
  "apiType": "rest",
  "pattern": {
    "method": "GET",
    "path": "/api/v3/simple/price",
    "queryParams": { "ids": "bitcoin", "vs_currencies": "usd" }
  },
  "tags": ["cryptocurrency", "price", "bitcoin"],
  "description": "Fetches current Bitcoin price in USD"
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Patterns are stored locally in SQLite database (not shared across instances)
- Duplicate patterns are allowed (use unique descriptive names)
- Storage limited by available disk space
- Does not validate if pattern still works (saved at time of success)
tools.search_learned_patterns:
Searches for previously learned API patterns with intelligent matching and ranking.

WHEN TO USE:
- Before making an API call (check if similar call was successful before)
- User asks for data you've fetched in previous sessions
- To find previously tested API patterns by keywords or tags
- When explore_rest_patterns finds nothing (check learned patterns instead)
- To discover what API calls are known to work

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Search completed
- patterns (array): Matching patterns sorted by relevance and usage count
- totalFound (number): Total number of matches found

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- patterns[0]: Most relevant/frequently used pattern (try this first)
- Each pattern includes: name, service, apiType, pattern structure, tags
- usageCount: How many times this pattern was used (higher = more proven)
- lastUsed: When pattern was last successfully used
- Use pattern.pattern field directly with call_rest_api or call_graphql

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "coingecko",
  "tags": ["bitcoin", "price"],
  "query": "get bitcoin price",
  "apiType": "rest",
  "limit": 5
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only finds patterns saved via save_api_pattern (empty if none saved)
- Returns empty array if no patterns match search criteria
- Fuzzy search may miss exact matches (try different keywords/tags)
- Patterns are not automatically validated (may be stale if API changed)
tools.get_service_stats:
Gets pattern learning statistics showing which API patterns have been learned and their success rates.

WHEN TO USE:
- To check pattern learning statistics (how many patterns saved, success rates)
- To see top performing API patterns
- To understand which services have learned patterns
- To get service-specific pattern statistics
- When deciding whether to use a learned pattern vs exploring new endpoints

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Whether stats retrieval succeeded
- stats (object): Pattern learning statistics including:
  - totalPatterns: Total number of learned patterns
  - byService: Pattern count per service
  - byApiType: Pattern count by type (REST/GraphQL)
  - totalUsages: Total times patterns have been used
  - avgSuccessRate: Average success rate across all patterns
- topPatterns: Array of top performing patterns with success rates

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- Use topPatterns to find proven API call patterns
- High usageCount indicates frequently used patterns
- High successRate indicates reliable patterns
- Use search_learned_patterns to find specific patterns by criteria
- Use discover_datasets to see available services (not this tool)

COMPLEMENTARY TOOLS:
- discover_datasets: Get service catalog with capabilities
- search_learned_patterns: Find patterns by service/tags/query
- get_system_health: Check real-time service health

EXAMPLE USAGE:

Get global pattern statistics:
{}

Get patterns for specific service:
{
  "service": "datadog"
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only shows learned patterns (not all possible API calls)
- Statistics are based on historical usage
- Does not show service catalog (use discover_datasets instead)
- Pattern success rates may be outdated if API changed
tools.get_system_health:
Gets comprehensive health status of the MCP server including services, cache, and pattern learning.

WHEN TO USE:
- Before making critical API calls (check if services are available)
- After experiencing errors (diagnose system state)
- To understand system capacity (cache size, pattern count)
- When troubleshooting performance issues (check latencies)
- To proactively inform users of service outages
- At the start of a workflow (ensure all required services are up)

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- success (boolean): Whether health check completed successfully
- health (object): Complete health report containing:
  - status: "healthy" | "degraded" | "down" (overall system status)
  - timestamp: When the health check was performed
  - services: Per-service health with latency and status
  - cacheStats: Cache statistics (entries, size)
  - patternLearning: Pattern statistics (total patterns, usage, success rate)
  - uptime: Server uptime in milliseconds

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- status="healthy": All services operational, proceed normally
- status="degraded": Some services slow/down, may need fallbacks
- status="down": Critical services unavailable, inform user
- services[x].status="up": Service is responsive
- services[x].status="degraded": Service is slow (>80% of timeout)
- services[x].status="down": Service is unreachable
- services[x].latency: Response time in ms (higher = slower)
- cacheStats.entries: Number of cached items (higher = better performance)
- patternLearning.totalPatterns: Learned patterns available for reuse
- patternLearning.avgSuccessRate: Success rate of learned patterns (0.0-1.0)

EXAMPLE USAGE:
Check full health with service pings:
{
  "includeServiceCheck": true,
  "timeout": 5000
}

Quick health check without service pings:
{
  "includeServiceCheck": false
}

LIMITATIONS:
- Service health checks add latency (5-10 seconds for multiple services)
- Lightweight health endpoints may not reflect full service health
- Does not check authentication credentials (only connectivity)
- Cache stats reflect current state only (no historical data)
- Pattern learning stats are aggregated (not real-time per pattern)
tools.get_response_statistics:
Get response size statistics for API endpoints tracked by the Response Size Manager.

WHEN TO USE:
- To understand typical response sizes for endpoints
- To investigate which endpoints return large responses
- To verify that size tracking is working
- To get historical data for capacity planning

WHAT IT RETURNS:
- statistics (array): List of endpoint statistics with:
  - endpoint: The endpoint key (service:method:path)
  - averageTokens: Average token count across all calls
  - maxTokens: Maximum token count observed
  - callCount: Number of times this endpoint has been called

HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:
- averageTokens gives you the typical response size
- maxTokens shows worst-case scenario
- callCount indicates confidence level (higher = more reliable average)
- Large maxTokens values indicate endpoints that may need optimization

EXAMPLE USAGE:
{
  "service": "datadog"
}

Or get all statistics:
{}

LIMITATIONS:
- Only shows statistics for endpoints that have been called since server started
- Statistics are in-memory only (reset on server restart)
- Maximum 10 historical entries per endpoint
tools.interpret_api_response:
Interprets API responses to extract meaning, identify issues, and suggest next steps.

**WHEN TO USE:**
- After receiving an API response that's complex or unclear
- To validate data quality before using it
- When you need to extract key information from nested responses
- To identify potential issues or anomalies in API data
- When deciding what to do next based on API response

**WHAT IT RETURNS:**
- success (boolean): Whether interpretation succeeded
- interpretation (object): Structured analysis with:
  - summary: Human-readable description of response
  - mainResult: The main data extracted from response
  - confidence: Score 0-1 indicating interpretation reliability
  - dataQuality: "high", "medium", or "low" quality assessment
  - anomalies: List of detected issues or unexpected values
  - suggestedFollowUp: Recommended next actions
  - keyFields: Important fields extracted from response
  - pattern: Identified response pattern (paginated_list, single_resource, etc.)

**HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:**
- confidence > 0.8: High confidence, safe to use data
- confidence 0.5-0.8: Medium confidence, verify key fields
- confidence < 0.5: Low confidence, investigate anomalies
- dataQuality "low": Response has critical issues, handle errors first
- Check anomalies array for specific problems to address
- Follow suggestedFollowUp for recommended next steps

**EXAMPLES:**

Example 1: Interpret paginated list response
```json
{
  "response": {
    "data": [{"id": 1, "name": "Product A"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Product B"}],
    "total": 100,
    "page": 1
  },
  "intent": "fetch product list"
}
```

Returns:
- summary: "Intent: fetch product list. Received array with 2 item(s). Identified as paginated list pattern."
- mainResult: [{"id": 1, "name": "Product A"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Product B"}]
- confidence: 0.9
- dataQuality: "high"
- suggestedFollowUp: [{"action": "fetch_next_page", "reason": "Paginated response may have more data"}]

Example 2: Interpret response with error
```json
{
  "response": {
    "error": "Not Found",
    "code": 404
  },
  "intent": "fetch user details"
}
```

Returns:
- summary: "Intent: fetch user details. Received object with 2 field(s)."
- confidence: 0.2 (low due to error)
- dataQuality: "low"
- anomalies: [{"field": "error", "severity": "critical", "message": "API returned error: Not Found"}]
- suggestedFollowUp: [{"action": "investigate_error", "priority": "high"}]

Example 3: Interpret with schema validation
```json
{
  "response": {"id": "123", "name": "Product", "price": "invalid"},
  "intent": "fetch product",
  "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "id": {"type": "string"},
      "name": {"type": "string"},
      "price": {"type": "number"}
    }
  }
}
```

Returns:
- confidence: 0.6 (reduced due to schema validation failure)
- anomalies: [{"field": "/price", "severity": "warning", "message": "Schema validation failed: must be number"}]

**LIMITATIONS:**
- Only interprets structure, doesn't understand business logic
- Schema validation requires valid JSON Schema format
- Pattern recognition limited to common REST/GraphQL patterns
- Confidence scores are heuristic, not statistically validated
- Cannot detect semantic errors (e.g., negative prices)
- Limited to synchronous interpretation (no async validation)
tools.summarize_multi_api_results:
Correlates data from multiple API responses, detects inconsistencies, and generates unified summary.

**WHEN TO USE:**
- After calling multiple related APIs (e.g., orders + inventory + shipping)
- To compare data across different services
- When validating data consistency between systems
- To merge results from different API calls
- When investigating discrepancies across services

**WHAT IT RETURNS:**
- success (boolean): Whether summarization succeeded
- summary (object): Unified analysis with:
  - summary: Human-readable description of findings
  - sourceCount: Number of API sources included
  - sources: List of source names
  - combinedData: Merged data from all sources
  - inconsistencies: Data mismatches between sources
  - correlations: Grouped data by correlation key (if provided)
  - dataQuality: Overall quality assessment
  - confidence: Reliability of the summary (0-1)
  - missingData: Fields that were expected but not found

**HOW TO INTERPRET RESULTS:**
- inconsistencies with severity "critical": Major data conflicts requiring attention
- inconsistencies with severity "warning": Minor discrepancies to investigate
- confidence > 0.8: High confidence in data correlation
- confidence < 0.5: Significant issues found, verify data manually
- Check correlations array to see how data was grouped
- Review missingData to identify gaps in API responses

**EXAMPLES:**

Example 1: Correlate order data from multiple services
```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "source": "orders_service",
      "response": {"orderId": "123", "status": "shipped", "total": 100}
    },
    {
      "source": "shipping_service",
      "response": {"orderId": "123", "status": "delivered", "trackingId": "TRACK123"}
    }
  ],
  "correlationKey": "orderId",
  "intent": "verify order fulfillment"
}
```

Returns:
- summary: "Correlated data from 2 sources (orders_service, shipping_service) using orderId"
- combinedData: {"orderId": "123", "status": "delivered", "total": 100, "trackingId": "TRACK123"}
- inconsistencies: [{"fields": ["status"], "values": {"orders_service": "shipped", "shipping_service": "delivered"}, "severity": "warning"}]
- correlations: [{"key": "123", "matchCount": 2, "sources": ["orders_service", "shipping_service"]}]

Example 2: Detect missing data
```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "source": "products",
      "response": {"id": "P1", "name": "Product A"}
    },
    {
      "source": "inventory",
      "response": {"id": "P1"}
    }
  ],
  "correlationKey": "id"
}
```

Returns:
- missingData: ["inventory.stock", "inventory.warehouse"]
- dataQuality: "medium"

Example 3: No correlation key (simple merge)
```json
{
  "results": [
    {"source": "api1", "response": {"users": 100}},
    {"source": "api2", "response": {"orders": 50}}
  ]
}
```

Returns:
- combinedData: {"users": 100, "orders": 50}
- inconsistencies: []

**LIMITATIONS:**
- Correlation requires consistent key naming across sources
- Cannot detect semantic inconsistencies (e.g., different units)
- Limited to structural comparison, not business logic validation
- Maximum 100 results recommended for performance
- Does not handle circular references in data
- Timestamps not automatically normalized

tools.resolve-library-id:
Resolves a package/product name to a Context7-compatible library ID and returns a list of matching libraries.

You MUST call this function before 'get-library-docs' to obtain a valid Context7-compatible library ID UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

Selection Process:
1. Analyze the query to understand what library/package the user is looking for
2. Return the most relevant match based on:
- Name similarity to the query (exact matches prioritized)
- Description relevance to the query's intent
- Documentation coverage (prioritize libraries with higher Code Snippet counts)
- Trust score (consider libraries with scores of 7-10 more authoritative)

Response Format:
- Return the selected library ID in a clearly marked section
- Provide a brief explanation for why this library was chosen
- If multiple good matches exist, acknowledge this but proceed with the most relevant one
- If no good matches exist, clearly state this and suggest query refinements

tools.split_tasks:
Break down complex tasks into independent subtasks, establishing dependencies and priorities.

## 1. **Granularity Control (Required Reading)**

- ### **Minimum Viable Task**

  Each subtask should be completable and verifiable by a single developer within **1–2 working days** (approximately 8–16 hours).

- ### **Maximum Complexity Limitation**

  A single subtask should not span multiple technical domains such as **frontend**, **backend**, and **database**.  
  If cross-domain work is required, split it into multiple subtasks.

- ### **Recommended Number of Tasks**

  Avoid splitting into more than **10 subtasks** at once.  
  If more are needed, submit them in prioritized batches (6–8 tasks per batch).

- ### **Recommended Task Length**

  Each split should not exceed **5,000 characters**.  
  If it does, divide and submit in multiple batches.

- ### **Depth Limitation**
  The task tree should not exceed **3 levels**:
  - **Level 1**: Functional Modules
  - **Level 2**: Main Processes
  - **Level 3**: Key Steps

## 2. **Task Splitting Example**

- Identify **core functionality points**, and create a subtask for each.
- Annotate each subtask with:
  - **Input/Output**
  - **Acceptance Criteria**
- If needed, provide **pseudocode**:
  - Only outline high-level logic and key steps.
  - Avoid providing complete source code.
- Check **dependencies** between subtasks and specify them in the `dependencies` field.
- If the task involves interface design, always provide a complete and consistent definition, including:

  - Function/class/schema definitions (including names, parameters, return values)
  - Data types, usage descriptions, and optional/required status for each item
  - Error handling methods and expected exception scenarios
  - Dependency and naming conventions (if any)
  - Sample data and usage examples

  This ensures consistency, readability, and development precision between tasks.

## 3. **Dependencies and Prioritization**

- Mark each subtask with its `dependencies` list.
- Automatically compute and enforce execution order based on the dependency graph to prioritize the **critical path**.

## 4. **Update Mode Explanation (`updateMode`)**

When you need to create a new task that is not related to the current task list, be sure to use `clearAllTasks` to avoid task confusion.

- `append`: Keep existing unfinished tasks and add new ones.
- `overwrite`: Delete all unfinished tasks, keep completed ones.
- `selective`: Smart-match and update tasks by name.
- `clearAllTasks`: Clear all tasks and automatically back up the current list.

---

## 5. **Strict JSON Rules**

- ### **No Comments Allowed**

  JSON does not support comments.  
  Any use of `#` or `//` will cause parsing failures.

- ### **Proper Escaping Required**
  All special characters (e.g., double quotes `\"`, backslashes `\\`) must be properly escaped,  
  or they will be considered invalid.

## 6. **Important Notes**

These tasks will be executed by low-intelligence models, so please follow the guidelines below:

- `Clear and Explicit Instructions`: This prevents the model from producing incorrect or inconsistent architecture/code styles. Provide clear commands or specifications.
- `Encapsulated Interfaces`: Each task runs independently. Define the interfaces clearly — such as function names, parameters, return values — so that other task-executing models can easily understand how to interact with or integrate these functions.
- `Dependencies`: If there are dependencies between tasks, define the interaction interfaces first. Tasks do not need to know each other's implementation, but must know how to interact with one another.

tools.add_task:
Add a single task to an existing plan within a project. This tool allows you to quickly add individual tasks to plans that already have some structure or tasks.

## When to Use add_task vs create_plan

**Use `add_task` when:**
- Adding incremental tasks to existing plans that already contain tasks
- A new requirement comes up during development within an active plan
- You need to add a standalone task to a populated plan
- You want to add a task with specific implementation details to an existing workflow
- The plan already has an established structure and you're extending it

**Use `create_plan` instead when:**
- Starting fresh planning for a new project phase or feature
- Working with empty plans that need initial task structure
- You need comprehensive task planning and breakdown
- Setting up the initial workflow for a project plan
- You want to organize multiple related tasks from scratch

**Important:** For empty plans or initial planning, always use `create_plan` first to establish the task structure, then use `add_task` for incremental additions.

**Parameters:**
- `projectName`: Project name or ID where the task should be added (required for multi-project architecture)
- `name`: Task name (1-100 characters)
- `description`: Detailed task description (minimum 10 characters)
- `notes`: Optional additional notes or special requirements
- `dependencies`: Optional array of task IDs this task depends on (within the same plan)
- `relatedFiles`: Optional array of files related to this task
- `implementationGuide`: Optional step-by-step implementation guide
- `verificationCriteria`: Optional verification standards for task completion

**Example usage:**
```json
{
  "projectName": "WebApp Development",
  "name": "Add user authentication",
  "description": "Implement JWT-based user authentication system with login/logout functionality",
  "notes": "Use bcrypt for password hashing, implement rate limiting",
  "dependencies": ["create-user-model-task-id"],
  "relatedFiles": [
    {
      "path": "src/auth/auth.service.ts",
      "type": "CREATE",
      "description": "Main authentication service"
    }
  ],
  "implementationGuide": "1. Install jwt library 2. Create auth service 3. Add middleware 4. Write tests",
  "verificationCriteria": "User can login/logout successfully, passwords are hashed, rate limiting works"
}
```

## Integration with Multi-Project Architecture

This tool integrates seamlessly with the multi-project task management workflow:
- Tasks are added to the currently active plan within the specified project
- Dependencies are resolved within the same plan context
- Created tasks are compatible with all other task management tools
- Supports project-specific workflows and plan organization

tools.scrape_url_html:
Use a URL to scrape a website using the ScrAPI service and retrieve the result as HTML. Use this for scraping website content that is difficult to access because of bot detection, captchas or even geolocation restrictions. The result will be in HTML which is preferable if advanced parsing is required.

BROWSER COMMANDS: You can optionally provide browser commands to interact with the page before scraping (e.g., clicking buttons, filling forms, scrolling). Provide commands as a JSON array string. Available commands:
- Click: {"click": "#buttonId"} - Click an element using CSS selector
- Input: {"input": {"input[name='email']": "value"}} - Fill an input field
- Select: {"select": {"select[name='country']": "USA"}} - Select from dropdown
- Scroll: {"scroll": 1000} - Scroll down (negative values scroll up)
- Wait: {"wait": 5000} - Wait milliseconds (max 15000)
- WaitFor: {"waitfor": "#elementId"} - Wait for element to appear
- JavaScript: {"javascript": "console.log('test')"} - Execute custom JS
Example: [{"click": "#accept-cookies"}, {"wait": 2000}, {"input": {"input[name='search']": "query"}}]

tools.record_context:
Record development context to memory. Call IMMEDIATELY after file changes.

WHEN TO USE:
- After making code changes (edits, additions, deletions)
- When solving bugs or implementing features
- Documenting design decisions or learning
- Capturing important development work

WHEN NOT TO USE:
- Do NOT record query processes or search operations
- Do NOT record information retrieval (use semantic_search instead)
- Do NOT record when just looking up existing information

WORKFLOW: Edit files → semantic_search → record_context (or update_context if similar exists) → Respond

Auto-detects: Git changes, context type, quality scores. Smart update for duplicates (v2.4.9).

List all tracked projects with statistics and activity information.

- Finding project IDs for other operations (e.g., export_memory_graph)
- Checking project activity and statistics

PARAMETERS:
- include_stats: Include detailed statistics (default: true)
- limit: Max projects to return (default: 50)

Returns: Project ID, name, path, language, framework, stats (contexts, sessions, last activity).
tools.get_context:
Retrieve full details of specific contexts by their IDs or find related contexts.

WHEN TO USE:
- Getting full content after seeing previews in list_contexts
- Viewing complete details from semantic_search results
- Finding contexts related to a specific context
- Retrieving multiple contexts at once

PARAMETERS:
- context_ids: Single ID (string) or multiple IDs (array)
- relation_type: Optional. Find related contexts (depends_on, related_to, fixes, implements, tests, documents)

Returns complete context data: id, content, type, files, metadata, tags, timestamps.
tools.semantic_search:
Search through both development memory AND indexed codebase files using hybrid semantic+keyword algorithm.

WHEN TO USE:
- Finding how similar bugs were fixed
- Searching for code examples or patterns
- Discovering related work in project history
- Learning from past solutions
- Querying project files for implementation details
- Finding code patterns across the entire codebase

IMPORTANT: This is a READ-ONLY operation for finding information. Do NOT use this to record new contexts - use semantic_search to FIND answers, then respond directly to users.

KEY PARAMETERS:
- query: What you're looking for (required)
- project_path/session_id/file_path: Filter scope
- type: Filter by context type (bug_fix, feature_add, etc.)
- limit: Max results (default: 10)
- similarity_threshold: Min relevance 0-1 (default: 0.5)

Returns results sorted by relevance with scores and metadata.
tools.list_contexts:
List development contexts in chronological order (newest first) for browsing project history.

WHEN TO USE:
- Browsing recent work in a project
- Reviewing what was done in a session
- Getting overview of project activity

WHEN NOT TO USE:
- Searching for specific content → use semantic_search instead

PARAMETERS:
- project_path/session_id: Filter by project or session
- limit: Max contexts (default: 20)
- since: Time filter (24h, 7d, 30d, 90d)
- type: Filter by context type (bug_fix, feature_add, etc.)

Returns contexts with previews, sorted by creation time (newest first).
tools.delete_context: Delete a recorded context by ID.
tools.update_context:
Update existing memory context to avoid duplicate records.

WHEN TO USE:
- User explicitly requests to update a previous memory
- AI discovers the same bug/issue was already recorded and needs updating
- Refining or correcting previously recorded information
- Avoiding duplicate memories for the same problem

WORKFLOW:
1. Search for existing related context using semantic_search
2. If found duplicate/related context, use update_context instead of record_context
3. This prevents memory clutter and maintains clean history

YOU SHOULD:
- Check for existing similar contexts before creating new ones
- Update existing context when solving the same problem again
- Preserve context history while keeping information current

tools.get_memory_status: Get memory system status: monitoring state, context count, cache stats.

tools.codebase:
Index codebase files into memory. Scans all files in the project directory and stores them for semantic search.

FEATURES:
- Recursive directory scanning with multi-language support
- Supports .gitignore and .augmentignore exclusion patterns
- Automatic binary file detection and skipping
- Incremental indexing based on file hashes (only changed files)
- Stores index in separate file_index table (doesn't pollute development memory)

EXAMPLES:
- First time setup: codebase({project_path: "/path/to/project"})
- Force reindex all files: codebase({project_path: "/path/to/project", force_reindex: true})
- After code changes: Run again to update index for semantic_search

EXCLUDED BY DEFAULT:
- node_modules/, .git/, dist/, build/, *.log, *.tmp
- Binary files (images, executables, etc.)
- Files matching .gitignore and .augmentignore patterns

Use semantic_search to query indexed files after indexing.
tools.delete_codebase_index:
Delete codebase index for a project. Removes all indexed files and related indexing sessions.

WHEN TO USE:
- Cleaning up after project deletion or move
- Resetting index to rebuild from scratch
- Freeing up disk space
- Removing outdated or corrupted index

EXAMPLE:
delete_codebase_index({project_path: "/path/to/project"})

Note: This only deletes the file index, not your development memory contexts.

tools.getNetworks: List every blockchain network DexPaprika indexes, each row carrying its network id (slug), 24h volume, transaction count, and pool count. Read-only and keyless. Start here (or getCapabilities) to get the exact network slug that nearly every other tool requires as its 'network' argument. Use for 'which chains do you support?', 'is Base/Solana/Arbitrum covered?', or 'what is the slug for Polygon?'. Returns the full array with no pagination or sorting; takes no parameters beyond a short rationale. For platform-wide totals rather than a per-network list use getStats.
tools.getCapabilities: Get the static agent onboarding guide for this server: supported workflows, network name synonyms (mapping words like 'eth' to the canonical slug 'ethereum'), recommended call sequences, and common pitfalls. Read-only and keyless. Read it once at the start of a session before your first query, or when asked 'how do I use this API?', 'what order should I call things in?', or 'which slug maps to eth?'. This returns onboarding docs, not live market data; for the actual list of network slugs use getNetworks, and for coverage totals use getStats. Takes no parameters beyond a short rationale.
tools.getNetworkDexes: List the DEXes (exchanges) operating on one network, such as Uniswap on ethereum or Raydium on solana, returned under 'dexes' with page_info (page, total_pages). Read-only and keyless. Use for 'which DEXes are on Base?', 'does Solana have Orca?', or to get a dex id to feed into getDexPools. Scope is a single network; call getNetworks first for the slug. Params: network (required slug); limit (default 10, max 100); page (default 1, 1-indexed); sort_by (only 'pool'; legacy alias order_by); sort_dir 'asc' or 'desc' (default 'desc'; legacy alias sort).
tools.getNetworkPools: Get the top liquidity pools across a whole network, ranked by 24h volume by default, returned under 'results' with has_next_page and next_cursor. Read-only and keyless. This is the primary chain-wide pool discovery tool. Use for 'biggest pools on ethereum', 'top trading pairs on Base', or 'most active pools on Solana'. Narrow to one exchange with getDexPools, or apply numeric/time filters with getNetworkPoolsFilter. Params: network (required slug); limit (default 10, max 100); cursor (pass previous next_cursor to page); sort_by (default 'volume_usd_24h', canonical *_24h fields, alias order_by); sort_dir 'asc' or 'desc' (default 'desc', alias sort).
tools.getDexPools: Get the pools belonging to one specific DEX on one network, e.g. all Uniswap v3 pools on ethereum, returned under 'pools' with page_info. Read-only and keyless. Narrower than getNetworkPools (a single exchange, not the whole chain). Use for 'show me Raydium pools', 'top pairs on PancakeSwap', or 'liquidity on Orca'. Get the dex id from getNetworkDexes or search first. Params: network (required slug); dex (required id, e.g. 'uniswap_v3'); limit (default 10, max 100); page (default 1); sort_by one of 'volume_usd','price_usd','transactions','last_price_change_usd_24h','created_at' (default 'volume_usd', alias order_by); sort_dir 'asc'/'desc' (default 'desc', alias sort).
tools.getNetworkPoolsFilter: Get pools on one network filtered by numeric thresholds, returned under 'results' with has_next_page and next_cursor. Read-only and keyless. Choose this over getNetworkPools when the user gives numeric constraints or a time window. Use for 'pools over $1M liquidity on Base', 'pools created in the last 24h', or 'high-volume low-liquidity pairs'. Optional filters (AND-combined): volume_24h_min/max, volume_7d_min/max, liquidity_usd_min/max, txns_24h_min, created_after/created_before (Unix timestamps). Also network (required); limit (default 50, max 100); cursor to page; sort_by (default 'volume_usd_24h', alias order_by); sort_dir asc/desc (default 'desc', alias sort).
tools.getPoolDetails: Get the full current snapshot for one pool by address: its two tokens, current price, liquidity/TVL, 24h volume, and transaction counts, returned as a single pool object (not a list). Read-only and keyless. Use after search or getNetworkPools surfaces a pool, or for 'price/TVL of this pool?' or 'details for pool 0x...'. Returns live values only; for historical candles use getPoolOHLCV, and for the raw swap feed use getPoolTransactions. Params: network (required slug); pool_address (required, e.g. '0x88e6a0c2ddd26feeb64f039a2c41296fcb3f5640'); inversed (optional bool, default false, flips the token price ratio to token1/token0).
tools.getPoolOHLCV: Get historical OHLCV candles (open, high, low, close, volume) for one pool over a time range, returned as a time-series array. Read-only and keyless. Use for 'price history of this pair', 'hourly chart for the last week', 'candles since Jan 1', or backtesting; for the single current price use getPoolDetails instead. Params: network (required); pool_address (required); start (required; Unix timestamp, RFC3339, or yyyy-mm-dd); end (optional, capped to 1 year after start); interval one of '1m','5m','10m','15m','30m','1h','6h','12h','24h' (default '24h'); limit (default 100, max 366 candles); inversed (optional bool, default false).
tools.getPoolTransactions: Get one pool's recent individual swap transactions, newest first, returned under 'transactions' (paginate with page, or a cursor). Read-only and keyless. These are per-trade records, not aggregated candles (use getPoolOHLCV) or a summary snapshot (use getPoolDetails). Use for 'recent trades on this pool', 'who swapped in the last hour', or 'raw transaction feed'. Params: network (required); pool_address (required); limit (default 10, max 100); page (default 1, up to 100 pages) or cursor (a transaction id); from (optional Unix seconds, inclusive, capped to the last 7 days); to (optional Unix seconds, exclusive, must be after from).
tools.getTokenDetails: Get one token's data and metadata by contract address on one network: multi-timeframe price and volume metrics, plus name, website, Twitter, and Telegram links, returned as a single token object. Read-only and keyless. Use for 'price and volume for 0x... on Base' or 'tell me about this token'. If you only have a symbol like WETH, call search first to resolve the address and network. For many tokens' prices at once use getTokenMultiPrices; for the pools holding this token use getTokenPools. Params: network (required slug); token_address (required contract address, e.g. 'JUPyiwrYJFskUPiHa7hkeR8VUtAeFoSYbKedZNsDvCN' on solana).
tools.getTokenPools: Get the liquidity pools that contain a specific token on one network, returned under 'results' with has_next_page and next_cursor. Read-only and keyless. Use for 'which pools hold WETH on ethereum?' or 'liquidity venues for 0x...'. Network-scoped, so run search first if unsure of the network; unknown addresses return empty results, not an error. For the token's own price use getTokenDetails. Params: network (required); token_address (required); limit (default 10, max 100); cursor to page; sort_by (default 'volume_usd_24h', alias order_by); sort_dir asc/desc (default 'desc', alias sort). Extra params such as inversed or paired_token_address are unsupported and error.
tools.getTokenMultiPrices: Get current USD prices for up to 10 tokens on the same network in one batched call, returned as a prices array plus a missing_tokens list. Read-only and keyless. Tokens that cannot be priced come back in missing_tokens rather than being dropped, so check that list for partial failures. Use for 'prices for these tokens', 'compare the price of X, Y and Z', or building a portfolio/dashboard snapshot. For one token with full metadata and multi-timeframe stats use getTokenDetails. Params: network (required slug, all tokens must share it); tokens (required array of 1 to 10 contract addresses).
tools.filterNetworkTokens: Get tokens on one network matching numeric thresholds, returned under 'results' with has_next_page and next_cursor. Read-only and keyless. Choose this over getTopTokens when the user gives numeric constraints or a time window. Use for 'tokens with FDV over $10M on Base', 'newly created tokens today', or 'low-liquidity high-volume tokens'. Optional filters (AND-combined): volume_24h_min/max, liquidity_usd_min/max, fdv_min/max, txns_24h_min, created_after/created_before (Unix timestamps). Also network (required); limit (default 50, max 100); cursor to page; sort_by (default 'volume_usd_24h', alias order_by); sort_dir asc/desc (default 'desc', alias sort).
tools.getTopTokens: Get the top tokens on one network ranked by volume, liquidity, transactions, FDV, or 24h price change, returned under 'results' with has_next_page and next_cursor. Read-only and keyless. Use for 'top gainers on Solana', 'highest-volume tokens on Base', or 'biggest tokens by FDV on ethereum'. For arbitrary numeric filters or a time window use filterNetworkTokens instead. Params: network (required slug); limit (default 50, max 100); cursor (pass previous next_cursor to page); sort_by (default 'volume_usd_24h', alias order_by), noting that ranking by raw price is unsupported and silently falls back to volume; sort_dir asc/desc (default 'desc', alias sort).
tools.search: Search across ALL networks at once for tokens, pools, and DEXes by name, symbol, or address, returning three arrays: 'tokens', 'pools', and 'dexes'. Read-only and keyless. This is the cross-chain entry point when you do not yet know which network something lives on; once you have a network slug from the results, switch to the network-scoped tools. Use for 'find PEPE', 'what is the address for USDC', or 'which chain is this token on?'. No matches returns empty arrays, not an error. Params: query (required; a name, symbol, or contract address, e.g. 'uniswap', 'bitcoin', or '0x...'); limit (optional, caps results per category, applied client-side).
tools.getStats: Get platform-wide totals for DexPaprika: the number of networks, DEXes, pools, and tokens indexed, returned as a single summary object. Read-only and keyless. Use for 'how much data do you cover?', 'how many chains or pools total?', or a one-line coverage summary. These are ecosystem-wide counts, not per-network figures; use getNetworks for the per-chain breakdown, or getCapabilities for onboarding docs. Takes no parameters beyond a short rationale.

tools.get_weather_summary: Get a combined weather overview for a location in a SINGLE call. Best for broad questions like "What's the weather like in Seattle?", "Is it safe to hike today?", or "Give me a weather rundown". Aggregates current conditions, forecast, and active alerts by default, and can also include air quality and lightning. Provide the location as coordinates (latitude+longitude), a saved location_name, or a free-text city_name. For a single specific data product (just the forecast, just alerts, etc.), call that specialized tool directly. Sections that are unavailable for a location (e.g. US-only alerts abroad) are noted rather than failing the whole summary.
tools.get_forecast: Get future weather forecast for a location (global coverage). Use this for upcoming weather predictions (e.g., "tomorrow", "this week", "next 7 days", "hourly forecast"). Returns forecast data including temperature, precipitation, wind, conditions, and sunrise/sunset times. Supports both daily and hourly granularity. Automatically selects best data source: NOAA for US locations (more detailed), Open-Meteo for international locations. For current weather, use get_current_conditions. For past weather, use get_historical_weather. Provide the location in ONE of three ways: coordinates (latitude+longitude), a saved location name (location_name="home"), or a free-text city name (city_name="Paris, France") which is geocoded automatically. If this tool returns an error, check the error message for status page links and consider using check_service_status to verify API availability.
tools.get_current_conditions: Get the most recent weather observation for a location (global coverage). Use this for current weather or when asking about "today's weather", "right now", or recent conditions without a specific historical date range. Returns NOAA station observations for US locations and Open-Meteo model data for international locations. Optionally includes fire weather indices (Haines Index, Grassland Fire Danger, Red Flag Threat) when requested. Provide the location as coordinates (latitude+longitude), a saved location_name, or a free-text city_name. For specific past dates or date ranges, use get_historical_weather instead. If this tool returns an error, check the error message for status page links and consider using check_service_status to verify API availability.
tools.get_alerts: Get active weather alerts, watches, warnings, and advisories for a location (US only). Use this for safety-critical weather information when asked about "any alerts?", "weather warnings?", "is it safe?", "dangerous weather?", or "weather watches?". Returns severity, urgency, certainty, effective/expiration times, and affected areas. Provide the location as coordinates (latitude+longitude), a saved location_name, or a free-text city_name. For forecast data, use get_forecast instead. If this tool returns an error, check the error message for status page links and consider using check_service_status to verify API availability.
tools.search_location: Search for locations by name to get coordinates for weather queries. Uses Nominatim (OpenStreetMap) for excellent coverage of cities, towns, villages, and hamlets worldwide. Use this when the user provides a location name instead of coordinates (e.g., "Paris", "New York", "Tokyo", "San Francisco, CA", "Small Village, County"). Returns location matches with coordinates, timezone, elevation, and other metadata. Enables natural language location queries like "What's the weather in Paris?" by converting location names to coordinates.
tools.check_service_status: Check the operational status of the NOAA and Open-Meteo weather APIs. Use this when experiencing errors or to proactively verify service availability before making weather data requests. Returns current status, helpful messages, and links to official status pages.
